catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alban-isidor-:
Alban Isidor Stolz was a German Catholic theologian and widely read religious author, born at Bühl in Baden in 1808 and dead at Freiburg in 1883. After studying law briefly, he turned to theology at Freiburg, passed through a period of doubt, and regained his faith while studying language and literature at Heidelberg. He then entered the seminary at Freiburg to prepare for the priesthood.

Stolz won lasting fame as a writer of popular religious books rather than as a scholar. His command of language and his eye for human nature set his work apart. His Legende, a book of saints' legends called the Christian starry heaven, ran through many editions, and his short moral and argumentative pieces were gathered as Kleinigkeiten. His collected works filled nineteen volumes, published at Freiburg between 1871 and 1895.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chelm-and-bel:
An entry on the Diocese of Chelm and Belz, a Greek-Ruthenian-rite diocese in Russian Poland, directly subject to the Holy See. Founded in 1592, it belonged to the Uniat Church, Eastern churches in union with Rome, and was the last of them to hold out against persecution by the Russian government. In 1841 Bishop Felix Szumborski agreed to restore the rite used before the union, but, warned by the pope, he withdrew the order.

A struggle followed between Church and civil power. Every priest who stayed true to his faith was exiled while the faithful were oppressed. Through persecution and schism, a break from unity, the diocese was in effect wiped out, though its name lived on in Church lists. The entry records the end of a diocese that resisted longer than any sister see under Russian rule.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-martin-a:
John Martin Augustine Scholz was a German Orientalist and biblical critic of the early nineteenth century. Born near Breslau in 1794, he studied at Breslau's Catholic gymnasium and university. He took his doctorate in theology at Freiburg in 1817. He studied Persian and Arabic in Paris under Silvestre de Sacy, while collating Greek, Latin, Arabic, and Syriac manuscripts of the New Testament.

Traveling through London, France, Switzerland, Italy, Egypt, Palestine, and Syria in search of biblical evidence, he was ordained at Breslau in 1821. He became professor of exegesis at Bonn, a chair he held until his death in 1852. His critical Greek New Testament of 1830 and 1836 was full of erudition but marred by faulty classification and critical slips. His introduction to the Scriptures, biblical archaeology, and travel accounts rounded out a busy scholarly life.
